subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Diffusion is best described as the movement of particles:
options: From a high to a low concentration down a concentration gradient
Of water only across a membrane
From a low to a high concentration using energy
questions.explain: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration, down the gradient, and is passive.

questions.q: Fish gills have many thin filaments with a very rich blood supply. The rich blood supply helps gas exchange by:
options: Reducing the surface area of the gills
Removing absorbed oxygen quickly to keep a steep concentration gradient
Stopping water from entering the fish
Providing energy for active transport of oxygen
questions.explain: A good blood supply carries oxygen away rapidly, maintaining a steep concentration gradient for diffusion.

questions.q: Which process always requires energy released by respiration?
options: Diffusion of oxygen into a cell
Osmosis of water into a cell
Active transport of ions into a root hair cell
Evaporation of water from a leaf
questions.explain: Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient and needs energy from respiration.

questions.q: Animal cells placed in pure water can burst, but plant cells in pure water do not. This is because plant cells have a:
questions.explain: The cell wall is strong and resists the pressure as water enters, stopping the plant cell bursting.

questions.q: Which gas diffuses from the alveoli into the blood?
questions.explain: Oxygen diffuses from the high concentration in the alveoli into the blood.

questions.q: Which side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood?
questions.explain: The right side of the heart receives and pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

questions.q: A piece of potato is placed in pure (distilled) water. What is most likely to happen to its cells?
options: Water enters the cells by osmosis and they become turgid
Water leaves the cells and they become flaccid
Sugar diffuses out of the cells
questions.explain: Pure water is more dilute than the cell contents, so water enters by osmosis, making cells turgid and increasing mass.

questions.q: Which natural pacemaker in the heart sets the resting heart rate?
options: A group of cells in the right atrium
questions.explain: A group of cells in the right atrium acts as the pacemaker, controlling heart rate.

questions.q: In a leaf, which structures allow gases to enter and leave?
questions.explain: Stomata are small pores, mainly on the lower leaf surface, that allow gas exchange.

questions.q: What does 'partially permeable' mean when describing a cell membrane in osmosis?
options: It lets water through but not larger solute molecules
It lets all substances pass through equally
It blocks water but allows large molecules through
It only allows movement when energy is supplied
questions.explain: A partially permeable membrane allows water molecules through but not larger solute molecules such as sugars.

questions.q: Put these airways in the order air passes through them.
questions.explain: Air passes from the trachea into the bronchi, then bronchioles, and finally the alveoli.

questions.q: Root hair cells are well adapted for absorbing water because they:
options: Carry out active transport of water
Have a large surface area and a thin cell wall
questions.explain: A large surface area and thin wall maximise water uptake by osmosis (water is never moved by active transport).

questions.q: Why do capillaries have walls that are one cell thick?
options: To allow efficient exchange of substances by short diffusion distance
questions.explain: Thin capillary walls give a short diffusion path for exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste.

questions.q: What lines the trachea and bronchi to trap dust and microbes?
questions.explain: Sticky mucus traps particles and cilia sweep it away from the lungs.

questions.q: The leaves of plants have many stomata and air spaces. This mainly increases the rate of gas exchange by:
options: Using active transport to pull gases in
Increasing the surface area for diffusion of gases
Pumping carbon dioxide against its gradient
Heating the leaf to speed up reactions
questions.explain: Stomata and internal air spaces increase the surface area available for gases to diffuse in and out.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows blood flow through the right side of the heart?
options: Vena cava then right atrium then right ventricle then pulmonary artery
Aorta then left atrium then right ventricle then lungs
Pulmonary vein then right ventricle then aorta
Right atrium then left ventricle then vena cava
questions.explain: Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle and out via the pulmonary artery.

questions.q: During exhalation, what does the diaphragm do?
options: Relaxes and moves up, decreasing chest volume
questions.explain: On breathing out the diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards, reducing chest volume and forcing air out.

questions.q: Which vessel returns oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
questions.explain: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the heart.

questions.q: Which is an adaptation of alveoli for efficient gas exchange?
options: Large surface area, thin moist walls and good blood supply
questions.explain: Alveoli have a large surface area, thin moist walls and rich blood supply to maximise diffusion.

questions.q: Why do gas-exchange surfaces such as alveoli need a good blood supply?
options: To maintain steep concentration gradients for diffusion
questions.explain: A good blood supply quickly removes diffused gases, keeping a steep concentration gradient.

questions.q: What is the role of the rings of cartilage in the trachea?
questions.explain: Cartilage rings hold the trachea open so air can always flow through.

questions.q: As an organism gets larger, its surface area to volume ratio:
questions.explain: Larger organisms have a smaller surface area to volume ratio, so they need specialised exchange surfaces and transport systems.
